title: Should I switch from traditional coding to AI (Vibe?) Coding or AI-based Game Engine?
author: KrysleQuinsen
selftext:
Seeing the surge of AI-Augment Game Engine, or even AI-based Game Engine lately, I have been wondering that if I should switch to AI coding? Originally I was planning to use AI for just the math, pesudo-code, and for content generation (image, model, animation, etc.

Long-short story, I have been using the same game engine as my last, abandoned game, that I made and released in 8 years ago.  And I recently kinda got my dream-game flame reignited.

However, I feel like my coding skill is starting to become one of my new-roadblock and frustration. 

While some of the mechanic is easily port-over or easily to work with. Some of the game mechanic, however, prove rather time consuming, I have been stuck doing one of the rather complex game mechanic (at least code-wise) for at least 4 months with no sight to finish just this mechanic yet.

comments.author: Vast_Emu_2346
comments.body:
Godot with codex or Claude code or antigravity is the answer. 

Do not buy into those "AI xyz" products that are entirely slopcoded and just worse versions made by snake oil sellers that are just worse than existing agentic tools from the big ai houses. 

You could probably even set up MCP and use deep seek in that way for even cheaper (like 10x from chagpt iirc for really similar quality as indie games aren't that hard to code)

replies.author: Hendo52
replies.body: I agree. Local LLM with MCP is difficult to setup. Real programming experience is great here and if OP wants to go hard in the long run, this is the foundational work that will pay the divedends. Smart first step. Frontier AI is great but cheap AI is where the party is going to be because running it for cents instead of dollars per hour is critical to being able to get a project rather than a feature done.

replies.author: Vast_Emu_2346
replies.body:
I'd still say that paying api costs for deepseek if you're not going for frontier models is way more goated than using fully local LLM. 

I'd avoid anything related to lovable or other firms similar to it

replies.author: Luna2442
replies.body: 100% this - codex is still the best bang for your buck imo

comments.author: count023
comments.body:
switch to orchestration. 

You dont write every bit of code yourself, but you design exactly how it works and what the milestones are and how to test it. explaint ot he AI how you want your mechanic to work, design it and iterate on the design with the AI until it comesout hte way you wanted it, then have it build htat. 

It's what i've been doing these last few months.

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
Same. Large, detailed plans. Review what the AI wants to do, and correct it. Ask it to hand you questions, sometimes you don't think of context it's missing. Code review. If something is off fix it as soon as you can. 

You don't want to find out after a week of vibe coding something that it had the whole idea wrong, but you weren't code reviewing to catch it.

comments.author: 300isAwesome69
comments.body: Yes if you want to stay relevant

comments.author: Prettypeachrec
comments.body:
Even ChatGPT 5.5 is miles better than it was 6 months ago.. and this is like bottom level code generation. Codex is brilliant if you can afford it. Claude is… well, Claude. 

My take, don’t spend ages re-learning code. Get the clanker to do it for you! 

Have fun with the game loop design and architecture. 

AI code is surprisingly much better than most people let on. ESPECIALLY if you already know somewhat what you’re doing with the code. 

Nowadays I don’t even use automated Codex/Claude I just get GPT5.5 to generate me copy/paste .cs files and I look over them before using, works better for me as I prefer knowing what code is coming and going.

Tried the automated Codex system plugged into Unity and to be honest it wasn’t for me. 

Regardless, don’t fall behind like most other devs on Reddit to stubborn to admit the that the robot is faster.. lol

replies.author: M4xs0n
replies.body: This is the way. And anyone who is telling you AI code is a mess and will break when you code a lot of mechanics for your game has no idea what he is talking about

replies.body:
Unity, ChatGPT and Blender (If I’m doing 3d) which I’m not mostly I work in 2d so for me my workflow is slim.

I use Suno for lobby/gameplay music loops and then some Unity Asset store SFX then I record Voice effects myself.

comments.author: meowsaygames
comments.body:
If you are a professional developer with solid programming and development experience, firstly, regarding engine selection, I think using commercial engines like Unity or Unreal Engine is a better choice because they have a complete ecosystem and technical support. 

Even though they are paid, reaching the charging threshold requires significant revenue, so as an individual developer, you shouldn't need to worry about engine fees. 

Secondly, regarding AI, I don't think it's necessary to abandon traditional programming and completely switch to AI. At this stage, the two methods can coexist and collaborate. Firstly, AI is still imperfect and constantly evolving. Currently, AI can serve as an efficiency-enhancing tool in your game development process. 

Perhaps in a few years, AI will become more powerful, and your traditional programming skills will still be very useful, better guiding AI to meet your needs. 

When AI becomes omnipotent, and anyone can command it to create something, then the question of "what to create?"—judging the value of AI-generated content—becomes extremely important.

comments.author: mallcopsarebastards
comments.body: it's kind of like askign if you should write a book with a pen and paper. There are better tools if the thing you're trying to do is go faster, but if you want to write it with a pen and paper that's perfectly legitimate as well. It's your project. Do what you want.

comments.author: Usual_Doughnut_4847
comments.body: Learn it. Here's the unsexy reason: something like 60%+ of people vibe coding right now have zero dev background, and they all hit the identical wall — the app works until it doesn't and they have no idea why. AI will happily generate a bug and then generate a confident, completely wrong explanation of that bug. Knowing the fundamentals is what lets you call BS on it. You don't need to grind LeetCode for two years — build small things, but force yourself to actually read and understand what the model hands you instead of paste-and-pray. Think of AI as a fast intern, not a senior engineer. The people who can direct it *and* check it are going to eat well.

comments.body: I mean, it is 2026... you may as well live like its 2026

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
What do you mean by "AI-Augment Game Engine" or "AI-based Game Engine"? Are you referring to those various scam tools that just incorporate a copilot-like bar into a shitty harness that happens to have a screen to display the editor for the game engine in question? Because those are all just using existing game engines. There is no "AI-based Game Engine". Those tools just make the game development  even more frustrating because crucial information from the engine's standard editor is not visible, which would allow for more explicit changes, by you, in the event you know what you're doing, rather than trying to get  AI to do the finer things for you.

AI helps a lot with game dev. Don't get me wrong. But it's going to drop the ball hard in a lot of places too, especially anytime it's something visual or spatial involved. It helps to be able to manually override whatever it's trying to do and to be able to follow along even when you don't feel the need to step in.

I do suggest going with one of the three big game engines though (not "AI-based" but just the most heavily supported/most flexible.) Unity/Godot/Unreal have the most longevity for you as a developer. There are smaller, more limited engines that are fairly popular too, but depend on the scope of games you're making, the platform you're making them for, or the genre they're in.

comments.author: Varrianda
comments.body: My advice is use an engine, but only as a way to display data and have the majority of the game be in either c# or cpp and create bespoke solutions for most things. Agents work better when they’re not constrained to a framework.

comments.author: Luna2442
comments.body: Full on vibe coding is still a recipe for disaster imo - if you dont know whats happening youre gonna write so much overengineered spaghetti youll have a much larger headache. Its all about balance.
